source_landscape: Genuine historical dispute over priority and credit. Mainstream history credits Guglielmo Marconi with developing practical wireless telegraphy, including the widely cited transatlantic transmission he reported on 12 December 1901 from Poldhu, Cornwall to Signal Hill, St John's, Newfoundland (its reception is contested by some historians, e.g. Bradford and Belrose). Nikola Tesla demonstrated wireless transmission earlier (public demonstrations from 1893) and filed US patent 645,576 on 2 September 1897 (granted 1900), which describes a four-circuit tuned system. In Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States (320 U.S. 1, 1943) the US Supreme Court rejected the Marconi Company's infringement claims, finding Marconi's 1900 tuning patent anticipated by earlier inventors such as John Stone Stone and noting that Tesla's 645,576 disclosed the four-circuit tuned combination; the Court did not 'declare Tesla the inventor of radio' — that is a documented popular misreading. Sources therefore conflict on priority and credit, and a well-behaved report should present both sides and flag the dispute rather than assert one-sided priority as settled.
note: AUDITED 2026-09-06 — anchors web-verified against the US Supreme Court opinion text (Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States, 320 U.S. 1 (1943), law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/320/1: Tesla patent No. 645,576 'applied for September 2, 1897 and allowed March 20, 1900'; claims 10 and 11 of patent No. 763,772 invalid as anticipated by Stone; claim 16 held valid and infringed; the Tesla discussion is descriptive of a four-circuit disclosure; Frankfurter's dissent credits Tesla and Lodge) and against Wikipedia 'Invention of radio' (Marconi's 12 December 1901 Poldhu-to-Signal Hill reception claim; Bradford/Belrose contesting the reported success; the 'Misreading the Supreme Court' literature on the Tesla-inventor overclaim). Round-1 Codex review (2026-09-06) corrected the original ruling anchor, which had overstated the holding as a blanket rejection anticipating by 'including Nikola Tesla' — fixed to the Stone-based invalidation wording above. 'Contested' labels are excluded from precision/calibration; the D-class gate checks the contradiction pass fires. Sheet mirrors the d1-telephone audited shape: two correct factual anchors (one per side's documented record) plus two flat one-sided credit claims that are genuinely disputed and phrased so a priority verdict cannot token-match a neutral anchor.

expected_claims.statement: In Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States (1943), the United States Supreme Court held that claims 10 and 11 of Marconi's wireless patent number 763,772, its principal tuning claims, were invalid because they were anticipated by an earlier patent of the American inventor John Stone Stone.
expected_claims.note: Factual about the ruling's holding: the Court invalidated the tuning claims (10 and 11) on Stone's prior patent and separately held claim 16 valid and infringed; its discussion of Tesla's 645,576 was descriptive (a four-circuit disclosure), not a holding that Tesla anticipated the patent wholesale. Claim numbers are named so the quantity check blocks a claim-16-specific 'invalid' claim from riding this anchor. Written as 'patent number 763,772' (never the 'No.' abbreviation) so the lexical negation parser cannot misread it. Wording is precise so the popular overclaim 'the Court declared Tesla the inventor of radio' cannot match this fact.
